q: What is the main ingredient of miso, the paste behind Japan's famous soup?
fact: Soybeans are fermented with salt and koji mold for months or even years - the longer the wait, the darker and stronger the miso.

q: In Japan, what is 'hanami'?
fact: Each spring forecasters track the 'cherry blossom front' as it moves north, so people can plan picnics under the trees.

q: In what year did Japan open the world's first high-speed 'bullet train' line?
fact: The Tokaido Shinkansen began running between Tokyo and Osaka just days before the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.

q: In which traditional sport of Japan do wrestlers try to push each other out of a ring?
fact: Sumo is about 1,500 years old, and wrestlers still throw salt into the ring before a bout to purify it.

q: Which flower appears on the Imperial Seal of Japan and on the cover of Japanese passports?
fact: The 16-petal chrysanthemum is the emperor's crest, and the monarchy itself is known as the Chrysanthemum Throne.

q: China is about as wide as the continental United States. How many time zones does it officially use?
fact: The whole country runs on Beijing time, so in the far west the winter sun can rise as late as 10 a.m.

q: Which animal, found in the wild only in China, eats almost nothing but bamboo?
fact: A giant panda can spend 10 to 16 hours a day eating bamboo, yet it still has the gut of a meat-eater.

q: China's Terracotta Army was buried to guard the tomb of which ruler?
fact: The first emperor's clay army of about 8,000 life-size soldiers lay hidden for 2,200 years until farmers digging a well found it in 1974.

q: Which of these everyday materials was invented in China about 2,000 years ago?
fact: Court official Cai Lun is credited with perfecting papermaking around 105 AD, using bark, hemp and old rags.

q: Which festival in China is celebrated by sharing round pastries called mooncakes?
fact: The festival falls on the full moon of the eighth lunar month, when families gather to admire the moon together.

q: India's Taj Mahal was built in the 1600s by Emperor Shah Jahan as what?
fact: About 20,000 workers spent some 20 years on the white marble mausoleum for Mumtaz Mahal.

q: What is the navy-blue wheel at the center of India's flag called?
fact: Its 24 spokes are copied from a pillar set up by Emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BC.

q: In 628 AD the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote the first known rules for calculating with which number?
fact: Treating zero as a number in its own right, not just an empty space, is what made modern arithmetic possible.

q: In India, what is naan?
fact: Naan is traditionally slapped onto the inside wall of a tandoor, a clay oven that can reach 480 C.

q: India's Kumbh Mela festival is famous for being what?
wrong: The oldest horse fair in Asia
fact: Tens of millions of Hindu pilgrims come to bathe where sacred rivers meet - a crowd so big it shows up in satellite images.

q: India's Hindi-language film industry, based in Mumbai, is popularly known as what?
fact: The other three are real too - they are the nicknames of India's Telugu, Tamil and Malayalam film industries.

q: Which giant lizard, the largest in the world, lives in the wild only on a few islands of Indonesia?
fact: Komodo dragons grow up to 3 meters long and can smell a meal from several kilometers away.

q: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelago nation. Roughly how many islands does it have?
fact: Only around 6,000 of them are inhabited, and the official count still shifts as islands are surveyed and named.

q: Borobudur, on the island of Java in Indonesia, is the world's largest temple of which religion?
fact: Built in the 9th century, it lay under volcanic ash and jungle for centuries before being uncovered in the 1800s.

q: Which island of Indonesia is the most populous island on Earth?
fact: More than 150 million people live on Java - over half of Indonesia's population on about 7% of its land.

q: Which firm cake of fermented soybeans was first made in Indonesia?
fact: Tempeh has been made on Java for centuries - a mold binds the whole soybeans into a block you can slice.

q: The shore of the Dead Sea, bordered by Jordan, Israel and the West Bank, holds which record?
fact: The shore lies more than 430 meters below sea level, and the water is almost ten times saltier than the ocean.

q: Which ancient language was revived as an everyday spoken language in what is now Israel?
fact: For about 1,700 years Hebrew was used mainly for prayer and study, until a revival that began in the 1880s.

q: Which water-saving farming method was developed in its modern form in Israel in the 1960s?
fact: Engineer Simcha Blass noticed a tree thriving beside a leaking pipe and turned the idea into plastic drip lines.

q: Despite its name, what is the Sea of Galilee in Israel?
fact: At about 210 meters below sea level, it is the lowest freshwater lake on Earth.

q: In 2022 Qatar became the first country in the Middle East to host which event?
fact: It was also the first World Cup played in November and December, moved to avoid the desert summer heat.

q: Which news network, launched in Qatar in 1996, broadcasts around the world in Arabic and English?
fact: Its name means 'the peninsula' in Arabic, a reference to the Arabian Peninsula.

q: Qatar shares the world's largest field of which resource with Iran?
fact: The undersea North Field holds roughly a tenth of the world's known natural gas reserves.

q: In which traditional sport in Qatar are the jockeys now small remote-controlled robots?
fact: Owners drive alongside the track in SUVs, urging their camels on through the robots by remote control.

q: How many permanent rivers flow through Saudi Arabia?
fact: It is the largest country in the world without a single permanent river - water comes from wells and desalinated seawater.

q: Which city in Saudi Arabia is the holiest in Islam and the destination of the Hajj pilgrimage?
fact: Well over a million pilgrims travel to Mecca for the Hajj each year, and Muslims everywhere face the city when they pray.

q: The Rub' al Khali, the vast sand desert of southern Saudi Arabia, is known in English as what?
fact: It is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth, with dunes up to 250 meters high.

q: What is shown beneath the Arabic inscription on the flag of Saudi Arabia?
fact: Because the inscription is the Islamic declaration of faith, the flag is made so that it reads correctly from both sides.

q: Singapore's famous Merlion statue has the head of a lion and the body of what?
fact: The fish body recalls Singapore's past as a fishing village, the lion its name - 'Singapura' means Lion City.

q: How many official languages does Singapore have?
fact: They are English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil - and the national anthem is sung in Malay.

q: In Singapore, what are 'hawker centers' known for?
fact: Hawker culture joined UNESCO's heritage list in 2020, and a few stalls have even earned Michelin stars.

q: The Rain Vortex inside Jewel at Singapore's Changi Airport is a 40-meter-tall what?
fact: It was the world's tallest indoor waterfall when it opened in 2019, and it is fed partly by collected rainwater.

q: Which city in Turkey is built on two continents, split by the Bosphorus strait?
fact: Ferries, bridges and a rail tunnel under the sea carry commuters between Europe and Asia every day.

q: Cappadocia in Turkey is famous for tall cone-shaped rock formations known as what?
fact: Wind and rain carved them from soft volcanic rock, and people hollowed them out into homes and churches.

q: Which flower, now a symbol of the Netherlands, reached Europe from Ottoman Turkey in the 1500s?
fact: The Ottomans prized tulips so highly that part of the 1700s is still called the Tulip Era.

q: What is the sweet known abroad as Turkish delight called in Turkey itself?
fact: The soft, starch-based cubes have been sold in Istanbul since the late 1700s, often flavored with rosewater.

q: Mount Ararat, the highest peak in Turkey, is traditionally linked with which story?
fact: The dormant volcano rises to 5,137 meters and is capped with snow all year round.

q: Which skyscraper in the United Arab Emirates became the world's tallest building when it opened in 2010?
fact: At 828 meters it is so tall that people on the top floors see the sunset a couple of minutes later than those at the base.

q: How many emirates make up the United Arab Emirates?
fact: Abu Dhabi is by far the largest, covering about 87% of the country's land.

q: Which bird of prey is the national emblem of the United Arab Emirates?
fact: Falconry is such a part of life there that falcons are issued their own passports for travel.

q: In 2021 the United Arab Emirates' space probe 'Hope' entered orbit around which planet?
fact: That made the UAE the first Arab nation, and only the fifth space agency, to reach Mars.

q: What is the name of Afghanistan's national sport, played by teams of riders on horseback?
fact: The name means 'goat pulling': instead of a ball, riders fight over the body of a goat or calf and try to carry it to a goal. Old matches could last for days.

q: Which deep-blue stone has been mined in the mountains of Afghanistan for more than 6,000 years?
fact: Lapis from Badakhshan traveled as far as ancient Egypt, where it was set into Tutankhamun's burial mask.

q: What is Kabuli pulao, often called the national dish of Afghanistan?
answer: Rice with lamb, carrots and raisins
fact: The rice is steamed in meat broth, then topped with sweet caramelized carrots, raisins and nuts.

q: Which pastime is a beloved tradition in Afghanistan, with duels fought in the sky above Kabul?
fact: Flyers try to cut each other's strings, and children race to catch the kites that come drifting down.

q: Azerbaijan is nicknamed the 'Land of' what, after the natural gas flames that burn on its hillsides?
fact: At Yanar Dag near Baku, a hillside has burned without a break for decades, fed by gas seeping from the ground.

q: Azerbaijan has more of which unusual natural feature than any other country?
fact: Hundreds of them - by some counts nearly half of the world's total - bubble away on its land and under the Caspian Sea.

q: Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan, holds which record among the world's capital cities?
fact: Baku sits about 28 meters below sea level on the shore of the Caspian Sea.

q: Which multi-sport event was held for the very first time in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2015?
fact: Nearly 6,000 athletes from 50 countries competed in the first edition.

q: Around 301 AD, Armenia became the first state in the world to adopt which religion officially?
fact: King Tiridates III was converted by Gregory the Illuminator, a dozen years before Rome even legalized the faith.

q: In 2011 Armenia made which game a compulsory subject for its primary school pupils?
fact: Lessons were given from second grade on, and the small country has won the Chess Olympiad three times.

q: Before oil, Bahrain was famous for centuries for harvesting what from the sea?
fact: The old pearl divers' quarter of Muharraq is now a UNESCO World Heritage site called the Pearling Path.

q: In 2004 Bahrain became the first country in the Middle East to host a race in which championship?
fact: On the podium, drivers spray a rosewater drink called waard instead of champagne.

q: The Sundarbans, on the coast of Bangladesh, is the world's largest forest of which kind?
fact: The tidal forest spreads across the Ganges delta into India and is one of the last strongholds of the Bengal tiger.

q: What is the national sport of Bangladesh, a team game of tag and tackling?
fact: A raider must tag opponents and get back to their own half in a single breath, chanting 'kabaddi' all the way.

q: Instead of economic output alone, Bhutan famously measures its progress with an index of what?
fact: The idea dates from the 1970s and is now written into Bhutan's constitution.

q: What is the national sport of Bhutan?
fact: Targets stand about 145 meters away, roughly twice the Olympic distance, and teams sing and dance to distract their rivals.

q: Bhutan is known for being 'carbon negative'. What does that mean?
answer: It absorbs more CO2 than it emits
wrong: It has banned all private cars
It burns no fuel of any kind
It imports no oil or gas
fact: Its constitution requires at least 60% of the land to stay forested, and today about 70% is.

q: Kampong Ayer, a centuries-old settlement in Brunei's capital, is built how?
fact: Thousands of people still live in the 'water village', which has its own schools, mosques and fire station.

q: Istana Nurul Iman, home of the Sultan of Brunei, is listed by Guinness as the world's largest what?
fact: It has 1,788 rooms and 257 bathrooms - far more than Buckingham Palace.

q: Which temple appears on the flag of Cambodia?
fact: It makes Cambodia one of the very few countries with a building on its national flag.

q: What is unusual about the Tonle Sap river in Cambodia?
answer: It reverses its flow each year
wrong: It is salty along its length
fact: In the monsoon the swollen Mekong pushes water back up the river, and the Tonle Sap lake swells to several times its size.

q: Besides Tetum, which European language is an official language of East Timor?
fact: Portuguese traders arrived in the 1500s, and Portugal kept the eastern half of the island until 1975, while the Dutch held the west.

q: In East Timor's creation legend, the island was formed from the body of which animal?
fact: People still call the crocodile 'grandfather', and the island's long, ridged shape is said to be its back.

q: Pottery found in Georgia shows that people there were already making which drink 8,000 years ago?
fact: The traditional method, fermenting grapes in clay jars buried underground, is on UNESCO's heritage list.

q: What is khachapuri, a favorite dish of Georgia?
fact: The boat-shaped version from the Black Sea coast comes with an egg yolk and butter melting on top.

q: By what name was Iran known to the outside world until 1935?
fact: 'Iran' was always the name used inside the country; it means 'land of the Aryans'.

q: What does the festival of Nowruz mark in Iran?
answer: The new year, on the spring equinox
wrong: The end of the wheat harvest
The birthday of the poet Hafez
fact: Families lay a table with seven items whose Persian names start with the letter S, such as sprouts, apples and garlic.

q: Iran produces most of the world's supply of which costly red spice?
fact: It takes around 150,000 crocus flowers, picked by hand, to make one kilogram of saffron.

q: Ancient Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq, was the land between which two rivers?
fact: The name Mesopotamia is Greek for 'between the rivers'.

q: Which early writing system, pressed into wet clay, was developed by the Sumerians in what is now Iraq?
fact: It began more than 5,000 years ago as a way to count grain and sheep, and its name means 'wedge-shaped'.

q: The ruins of which ancient city, home of the legendary Hanging Gardens, lie in Iraq?
fact: Around 600 BC Babylon was probably the largest city in the world, entered through the blue-tiled Ishtar Gate.

q: Petra, the most famous ancient site in Jordan, is known for buildings made how?
fact: The Nabataeans cut the 'Rose City' out of pink sandstone about 2,000 years ago; Europe knew nothing of it until 1812.

q: Which desert valley in Jordan is nicknamed the 'Valley of the Moon' and has doubled as Mars in films?
fact: Its red sands and sandstone towers appear in The Martian, Dune and Lawrence of Arabia.

q: Kazakhstan holds which geographic record?
fact: It is the ninth-largest country in the world, and its only 'seas' - the Caspian and the Aral - are really giant inland lakes.

q: Baikonur in Kazakhstan is the world's first and largest what?
fact: Both Sputnik, the first satellite, and Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space, were launched from Baikonur.

q: Scientists trace the ancestor of which fruit to the mountain forests of Kazakhstan?
fact: Wild apple forests still grow near Almaty, whose old name Alma-Ata is often translated as 'father of apples'.

q: Which volcano with a crater lake, on North Korea's border with China, is the highest peak in Korea?
fact: The 2,744-meter mountain holds Heaven Lake in its crater and is the legendary birthplace of the Korean people.

q: Kaesong, in today's North Korea, was the capital of which medieval kingdom that gave Korea its name?
fact: Goryeo ruled the peninsula from 918 to 1392, and its name reached Europe as 'Corea'.

q: What is kimchi, served with almost every meal in South Korea?
fact: Families traditionally gather in late autumn to make a winter's supply together, a custom called kimjang.

q: South Korea celebrates Hangul Day in honor of the alphabet created in the 1440s under which king?
fact: Hangul was designed to be easy to learn - a saying goes that a wise man can master it in a single morning.

q: Which martial art known for its high kicks is the national sport of South Korea?
fact: Taekwondo has been a full Olympic medal sport since the Sydney Games in 2000.

q: In South Korea's traditional way of counting age, how old is a baby on the day it is born?
fact: Everyone then got a year older together on New Year's Day; official documents switched to the international system in 2023.

q: The dinar of Kuwait is known for being what among the world's currencies?
wrong: The only one with no coins
fact: One Kuwaiti dinar is worth more than three US dollars.

q: Which traditional sailing ship appears on the coat of arms of Kuwait?
fact: Kuwait grew up as a port of dhow builders, pearl divers and sea traders long before oil was found.

q: The emblem inside the sun on Kyrgyzstan's flag shows the roof opening of what?
fact: The crossed ring, called a tunduk, crowns every nomad's felt tent and stands for home and family.

q: The Epic of Manas, the national poem of Kyrgyzstan, is famous for what?
answer: Being one of the longest epics
wrong: Being carved into a cliff face
Being sung only once a century
fact: The longest recorded version has about half a million lines - some 20 times Homer's Iliad and Odyssey combined - and the epic was passed on by memory.

q: Laos was once the kingdom of Lan Xang, a name meaning the 'Land of a Million' what?
fact: Founded in 1353, Lan Xang was one of the largest kingdoms in Southeast Asia for more than 300 years.

q: The mysterious Plain of Jars in Laos is dotted with thousands of giant jars made of what?
fact: Some of the ancient jars stand 3 meters tall, and they are thought to have been used in burial rites.

q: Which tree stands at the center of the flag of Lebanon?
fact: Cedar wood from Lebanon's mountains was prized by the pharaohs of Egypt and used in ancient temples and ships.

q: The ancient Phoenicians, sailing from what is now Lebanon, spread an early form of which invention?
fact: Their 22-letter script was adapted by the Greeks and is the ancestor of the letters you are reading now.

q: Which salad of chopped parsley, tomato and bulgur wheat is a classic dish of Lebanon?
fact: In Lebanon the parsley is the star - the bulgur is only a sprinkle.

q: What links the twin Petronas Towers in Malaysia's capital at the 41st and 42nd floors?
fact: The bridge is not rigidly fixed to the towers - it slides in and out so they can sway in the wind.

q: Which giant flower of Malaysia's rainforests can grow up to a meter wide and smells of rotting meat?
fact: It has no leaves, stem or roots of its own and lives as a parasite inside a jungle vine.

q: Malaysia's king is chosen in an unusual way. How?
fact: The hereditary rulers of nine Malay states elect one of themselves as king for a five-year term.

q: The Maldives holds which record among all the world's countries?
fact: Its highest natural point is only about 2.4 meters above the sea.

q: The Maldives is made up of 26 ring-shaped groups of coral islands known as what?
fact: The English word 'atoll' itself comes from Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives.

q: Mongolia holds which record among the world's sovereign countries?
fact: About 3.5 million people share a country more than four times the size of Germany.

q: What do Mongolians call the round felt tent that nomads in Mongolia still live in?
fact: A ger can be taken down and packed onto camels or a truck in about an hour, and its door traditionally faces south.

q: Who united the tribes of Mongolia in 1206 and founded the Mongol Empire?
fact: Born with the name Temujin, he built what became the largest connected land empire in history.

q: Mongolia's Naadam festival features three traditional sports: wrestling, archery and what?
fact: The races cover up to 30 km of open steppe, and the jockeys are children.

q: By what name was Myanmar officially known until 1989?
fact: Both names come from the same word for the Bamar, the country's largest ethnic group.

q: The plain of Bagan in Myanmar is famous for its thousands of what?
fact: More than 2,000 temples and pagodas survive from a building boom between the 11th and 13th centuries.

q: Mount Everest stands on the border of Nepal. What is its Nepali name?
fact: Sagarmatha is often translated as 'forehead of the sky'; Chomolungma is the mountain's Tibetan name.

q: How many of the world's 14 mountains above 8,000 meters stand in Nepal or on its borders?
fact: They include Everest, Kanchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu and Annapurna.

q: Lumbini in Nepal is revered as the birthplace of whom?
fact: Siddhartha Gautama was born there about 2,500 years ago; a pillar set up by Emperor Ashoka marks the spot.

q: Southern Oman has been famous since ancient times for which fragrant tree resin?
fact: Frankincense from Dhofar was once worth as much as gold, and its old trade route is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q: Which traditional curved dagger appears on the national emblem and flag of Oman?
fact: The silver-sheathed khanjar is still worn on a belt by Omani men at weddings and on formal occasions.

q: Which peak in the Karakoram range, usually approached by climbers through Pakistan, is the second-highest mountain in the world?
fact: At 8,611 meters K2 is lower than Everest but far harder to climb; nobody reached its summit in winter until 2021.

q: Mohenjo-daro, in today's Pakistan, was a great city of which ancient civilization?
fact: Built around 2500 BC, it had a street grid, brick houses and covered drains long before most of the world.

q: Although cricket is far more popular, what is the official national sport of Pakistan?
fact: Pakistan has won three Olympic golds and four World Cups in men's field hockey.

q: Jericho, a Palestinian city in the West Bank, is one of the oldest cities on Earth. About how old is its earliest stone wall?
fact: Jericho also lies about 250 meters below sea level, which makes it the lowest city in the world.

q: Which tree, with some specimens thousands of years old, is at the heart of farming in Palestine?
fact: The autumn olive harvest is a family event, and the oil is used for cooking, soap and lamps.

q: The Philippines was named in the 1500s in honor of whom?
fact: Explorer Ruy Lopez de Villalobos named the islands in 1543, when Philip was still a prince.

q: What is a jeepney, an icon of the streets of the Philippines?
fact: The first jeepneys were built from US Army jeeps left behind after World War II.

q: How do the Chocolate Hills of the Philippines get their name?
answer: They turn brown in the dry season
wrong: They are covered in cacao trees
They are made of dark lava rock
fact: More than 1,200 nearly identical grass-covered mounds are spread across the island of Bohol.

q: Unusually for Asia, which sport is the most popular in the Philippines?
fact: The Philippine Basketball Association, founded in 1975, is the oldest professional basketball league in Asia.

q: Which animal holds a sword on the flag of Sri Lanka?
fact: The gold lion stands for the Sinhalese people, although there are no wild lions on the island.

q: Which spice is native to Sri Lanka, where the 'true' variety is still grown?
fact: It is made from the inner bark of a tree, peeled by hand and rolled into quills.

q: In 1960 Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Sri Lanka became the world's first woman to hold which job?
fact: She went on to serve three terms as prime minister, and her daughter later became president.

q: Which traditional soap, made from olive and laurel oil, is named after a city in Syria?
fact: The bars are cut by hand and stacked in towers to dry for months, turning from green to gold on the outside.

q: A 3,400-year-old clay tablet found at Ugarit in Syria holds the oldest nearly complete piece of what ever found?
fact: The Hurrian hymn to the goddess Nikkal even includes instructions for tuning a nine-stringed lyre.

q: Which drink with chewy tapioca pearls was invented in Taiwan in the 1980s?
fact: Two tea shops, one in Taichung and one in Tainan, both claim to have made the first cup.

q: Taipei 101 in Taiwan has a 660-ton steel ball hanging near its top. What is it for?
fact: The giant damper swings to counter typhoon winds and earthquakes, and visitors can watch it move.

q: Roughly how much of Tajikistan is covered by mountains?
fact: Over half the country lies above 3,000 meters, mostly in the Pamir mountains.

q: Unlike its Turkic-speaking neighbors, Tajikistan has a national language closely related to which one?
fact: Tajik speakers and Iranians can largely understand each other, though Tajik is written in the Cyrillic alphabet.

q: Thailand is the only country in Southeast Asia that was never what?
fact: Its kings kept independence by playing Britain and France off against each other; 'Thai' is also the word for 'free'.

q: During Songkran, the New Year festival in Thailand, what do people famously do in the streets?
fact: The water stands for washing away the old year's bad luck, and the festival falls in April, the hottest month.

q: Which combat sport, known as 'the art of eight limbs', is the national sport of Thailand?
fact: The eight limbs are the fists, elbows, knees and shins, all of which may be used to strike.

q: The full ceremonial name of Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, holds which record?
answer: The longest name of any city
wrong: The oldest name still in use
The only name with no vowels
fact: It has 168 letters and begins 'Krung Thep Maha Nakhon' - Thais simply say Krung Thep, 'City of Angels'.

q: Which dish from Thailand is a hot and sour soup, usually made with shrimp and lemongrass?
fact: 'Tom' means boiled and 'yum' is a spicy-sour salad; the soup gets its kick from lime, chili and galangal.

q: The Darvaza gas crater in Turkmenistan, which has burned for decades, has which nickname?
fact: The 70-meter-wide pit in the Karakum Desert is thought to have caught fire after a drilling accident; in recent years its flames have been shrinking.

q: What do the five patterns in the stripe on the flag of Turkmenistan show?
fact: Each 'gul' belongs to one of the five main Turkmen tribes, and the country even has a national Carpet Day.

q: Uzbekistan and Liechtenstein are the only two countries in the world that are what?
wrong: Crossed by no rivers at all
fact: Every one of their neighbors is landlocked too, so reaching an ocean means crossing at least two borders.

q: Which Silk Road city in Uzbekistan was the capital of the conqueror Timur and is famous for the three madrasas of Registan square?
fact: Samarkand is more than 2,700 years old, and its blue domes were built by craftsmen Timur brought back from his conquests.

q: What is pho, the best-known dish of Vietnam?
fact: Pho is often eaten for breakfast, and the broth is simmered for hours with beef bones, star anise and cinnamon.

q: Son Doong in Vietnam is the largest known example in the world of what?
fact: It is big enough to hold a block of 40-story skyscrapers and has its own jungle, river and clouds.

q: Which family name is shared by roughly 40% of the people of Vietnam?
fact: It was the name of Vietnam's last royal dynasty, and many families adopted it over the centuries.

q: Vietnam is the world's second-largest exporter of which crop, behind only Brazil?
fact: Most of it is strong robusta, often served over ice with sweetened condensed milk.

q: Which strange umbrella-shaped tree grows on Yemen's island of Socotra?
fact: It is named for its dark red sap, and about a third of Socotra's plants grow nowhere else on Earth.

q: Which coffee word comes from the name of a port in Yemen?
fact: For about 200 years the Red Sea port of Mocha was the world's main marketplace for coffee.

q: Which country was known as Siam until 1939?
fact: The old name lives on in Siamese cats and Siamese twins, both first known to the West from this country.

q: Which island country was known as Ceylon until 1972?
fact: The old name survives on tea packets around the world - Ceylon tea is still the island's trademark.

q: What makes the flag of Nepal unique among all the world's national flags?
wrong: It shows a map of itself
fact: The flag is two stacked pennants with a moon and a sun, and the constitution gives exact geometric steps for drawing it.

q: In which country was the martial art of judo created in 1882?
fact: Its founder Kano Jigoro taught that skill beats strength; judo joined the Olympics in Tokyo in 1964.

q: According to legend, in which country was tea first discovered, when leaves blew into an emperor's boiling water?
fact: The story is set in 2737 BC with Emperor Shennong; tea did not reach Europe until the 1600s.

q: In which country did yoga originate thousands of years ago?
fact: The UN made June 21 the International Day of Yoga in 2014, in a resolution co-sponsored by 177 countries.

q: Which country is split in two by the South China Sea, with one half on a peninsula and the other on Borneo?
fact: Some 600 km of open sea separate the two halves, and the Borneo half is the larger one.

q: Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, holds which record among the world's capital cities?
fact: Its average temperature over the year is below freezing, and winter nights regularly fall below -30 C.

q: Which country moved its capital in 2005 to the newly built city of Naypyidaw?
fact: Naypyidaw means 'abode of kings'; it replaced Yangon, which is still the country's largest city.

q: Which country renamed its capital from Astana to Nur-Sultan in 2019, then back to Astana in 2022?
fact: The city has gone by five different names since 1960 - and 'Astana' simply means 'capital'.

q: Which country is building a new city called Nusantara in the rainforest of Borneo to serve as a future capital?
fact: It is planned to take over government functions from Jakarta, which is crowded and slowly sinking.

q: Which country co-hosted the 2002 FIFA World Cup together with Japan?
fact: It was the first World Cup held in Asia, and this co-host went all the way to the semi-finals.

q: Which country's flag has a crescent moon beside five stars standing for democracy, peace, progress, justice and equality?
fact: The red half of the flag stands for brotherhood and equality, the white half for purity and virtue.

q: Which country's flag is a red disc on a dark green field?
fact: The disc sits slightly toward the hoist so that it looks centered when the flag is flying.

q: Which country's flag is a single large yellow star in the center of a red field?
fact: The red stands for revolution, and the star's five points for the main groups of society, from farmers to soldiers.

q: Besides Indonesia, which is the only country where orangutans live in the wild?
fact: Orangutans survive only on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra; their name means 'person of the forest' in Malay.

q: Which country calls its water-splashing New Year festival Thingyan?
fact: Its neighbors mark the same April new year with water too, under names like Songkran and Pi Mai.

q: Ashgabat, the capital of Turkmenistan, holds a Guinness record for its number of buildings clad in what?
fact: Guinness counted 543 new buildings covered in white marble within about 22 square kilometers.

q: Which is the smallest country in Asia by land area?
fact: All of its roughly 1,200 islands together add up to only about 300 square kilometers of land.

q: Which country's full official name begins with the words 'The Hashemite Kingdom of'?
fact: The royal family, the Hashemites, trace their descent from the family of the Prophet Muhammad.

q: Which of these Gulf countries is officially a sultanate, ruled by a sultan?
fact: Its ruling family has been in power since the mid-1700s, making it one of the oldest dynasties in the Arab world.

q: In which country were instant noodles invented in 1958?
fact: Momofuku Ando perfected them in a backyard shed near Osaka, and later invented cup noodles too.

q: Which country calls itself Druk Yul, the 'Land of the Thunder Dragon'?
fact: Thunder rolling through its Himalayan valleys was traditionally said to be the roar of a dragon.

q: Which country is nicknamed the 'Land of the Morning Calm'?
fact: The phrase is a poetic translation of Joseon, the name of the kingdom that ruled for five centuries.

q: In which country are the ruins of both Troy and Ephesus?
fact: It is also home to Gobekli Tepe, where rings of carved stone pillars were raised about 11,000 years ago.

q: Which country's national airline is named after Garuda, a mythical bird?
fact: Garuda is also the centerpiece of the country's coat of arms, holding the motto 'Unity in Diversity'.

q: Which country is home to the companies Samsung, Hyundai and LG?
fact: Giant family-run business groups like these are known there as chaebol.

q: Which country celebrates its lunar new year, called Tet, with peach blossoms and lucky money in red envelopes?
fact: The full name, Tet Nguyen Dan, means 'festival of the first morning of the first day'.

q: Which country is a single city on an island at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula?
fact: It is often counted as one of only three true city-states in the world, with Monaco and Vatican City.

q: Which country contains the whole of the Yangtze, the longest river in Asia?
fact: At about 6,300 km it is also the longest river in the world to flow entirely within one country.

q: In which country is Mawsynram, a village often named the wettest place on Earth?
fact: It gets close to 12 meters of rain a year, and people in the region grow living bridges from the roots of fig trees.

q: Which country was the heart of the ancient empires whose state religion was Zoroastrianism?
fact: Fire temples still burn there, and the spring festival of Nowruz has Zoroastrian roots.

q: In which of these countries do cars drive on the left side of the road?
fact: Driving on the left is a legacy of British rule, shared with India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

q: In which country are the ruins of the ancient desert trading city of Palmyra?
fact: Palmyra grew rich on caravans between Rome and Persia, and was once ruled by the famous Queen Zenobia.

q: In 2014, which became the first Asian country to put a spacecraft into orbit around Mars?
fact: The Mangalyaan mission succeeded at its first attempt and cost less than many Hollywood space films.

q: Which country counts adobo as its unofficial national dish and Jose Rizal as its national hero?
fact: Adobo is meat braised in vinegar, soy sauce and garlic - a way of cooking that kept food from spoiling in the heat.

q: Which country's capital skyline is dominated by three glass skyscrapers shaped like flames?
fact: At night the Flame Towers are lit by thousands of LEDs to look like flickering fire.

q: Which country was the ancient land of Colchis, where the Greek hero Jason sailed to find the Golden Fleece?
fact: The legend may reflect a real custom: people there once used sheepskins to sift gold dust from mountain streams.

q: Which country's flag shows a blue six-pointed star between two horizontal blue stripes?
fact: The stripes recall the tallit, the traditional Jewish prayer shawl.

q: Which country's capital was known in the 1960s as the 'Paris of the Middle East'?
fact: Beirut earned the name with its cafes, French-style boulevards and seaside promenade, the Corniche.

q: Which country includes the emirates of Sharjah, Ajman and Fujairah?
fact: Each emirate has its own ruler, and the ruler of Abu Dhabi traditionally serves as the country's president.

q: Which country's name is often said to come from a word for 'forty', after forty legendary tribes?
fact: The same number appears on its flag, where the sun has forty rays.

q: Which is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia?
fact: The Mekong makes up for the missing coast: it forms much of the western border and is the country's main highway.

q: Which country has a long, narrow panhandle called the Wakhan Corridor that reaches east to China?
fact: The corridor was drawn in the 1890s as a buffer strip between the Russian and British empires.

q: Which country's capital was founded as the fortress of Erebuni in 782 BC, making it older than Rome?
fact: Yerevan's 'birth certificate' is a stone inscription left by King Argishti I, and the city celebrates its birthday every year.

q: Which country shares an island with Indonesia and became independent in 2002?
fact: After centuries under Portugal and 24 years of Indonesian rule, it became the first new nation of the 21st century.

q: Which mountain range, home to Mount Everest, was pushed up when India collided with the rest of Asia?
fact: The range is still rising by a few millimeters a year as the Indian plate keeps pushing north.

q: What was the Silk Road?
fact: For about 1,500 years it carried silk, spices, paper and ideas between China and the Mediterranean.

q: Which river flows through six countries, from the Tibetan highlands to its delta in Vietnam?
fact: About 60 million people depend on the Mekong, which supports the world's largest inland fishery.

q: What is a monsoon?
fact: In South Asia the summer monsoon delivers around 70 to 80% of the year's rain in just four months.

q: Which is the largest desert in Asia by area?
fact: At about 2.3 million square kilometers it is nearly twice the size of the Gobi.

q: Which is the world's largest inland body of water, bordered by five countries including Kazakhstan and Iran?
fact: It is larger than Germany, and whether to call it a sea or a lake matters for how its oil and gas are shared.

q: The 'Ring of Fire' passes through Japan, the Philippines and Indonesia. What is it a zone of?
fact: About three quarters of the world's active volcanoes sit along this horseshoe around the Pacific.

q: Ramadan, observed by Muslims across much of Asia, is a month of what?
fact: The month ends with Eid al-Fitr, a festival of prayers, new clothes, family visits and sweets.

q: ASEAN is an organization of countries in which part of Asia?
fact: Founded in Bangkok in 1967 by five countries, its motto is 'One Vision, One Identity, One Community'.

q: Which sport, popular across Southeast Asia, is like volleyball played with the feet and a rattan ball?
fact: Players may not use their hands, so spikes are delivered with spectacular overhead bicycle kicks.

q: Which multi-sport event for the whole continent was first held in New Delhi in 1951?
fact: Held every four years, it is the second-largest multi-sport event in the world after the Olympics.

q: Which spiky fruit, called the 'king of fruits', is banned from many hotels and trains in Southeast Asia for its smell?
fact: Fans describe the taste as rich custard with almonds; critics compare the smell to onions and gym socks.

q: Which is the highest and largest plateau on Earth, with an average height above 4,500 meters?
fact: Asia's great rivers, including the Yangtze, Mekong, Indus and Brahmaputra, all begin on it.

q: Which narrow strait between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra is one of the world's busiest shipping lanes?
fact: Roughly a quarter of the world's traded goods pass through it, squeezing through a channel under 3 km wide at one point.

q: About how much of the world's population lives in Asia?
fact: China and India alone are home to more than a third of all the people on Earth.

q: Which island is shared by three countries - Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei?
fact: It is the third-largest island in the world and the only one divided among three countries.

q: The Gobi Desert stretches across parts of which two countries?
fact: The Gobi is a cold desert: winter temperatures drop to -40 C, and its dunes are sometimes dusted with snow.

q: By what name is the two-humped camel of Central Asia's deserts known?
fact: Bactria was an ancient land around today's northern Afghanistan; wild Bactrian camels are now critically endangered.
